content: The quality of evidence supporting the recommendations for labor augmentation was rated as very low. The World Health Organization (WHO) has outlined several key research questions to address gaps in knowledge regarding labor augmentation. These include understanding the effects of herbal medications for preventing or treating delayed labor, evaluating interventions to reduce the use of herbal medications during labor, determining the safest maximum dose of oxytocin for labor augmentation, and comparing the outcomes of various augmentation methods in multiparous versus nulliparous women. Additionally, the optimal incremental rate of oxytocin infusion for labor augmentation needs to be identified. The ultimate goal of the WHO guideline is to improve the quality of care and health outcomes related to labor augmentation. Dissemination and implementation of the guideline are critical and require collaboration between the international community and local health services. The WHO Department of Reproductive Health and Research has adopted a formal knowledge-to-action framework to facilitate the dissemination, adaptation, and implementation of these guidelines. A list of priority actions was established during the WHO technical consultation, which will guide efforts to promote the guideline's adoption. The recommendations will be shared through a broad network of international partners, including WHO country and regional offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. A policy brief will also be developed for policymakers, program managers, and clinicians, and distributed through WHO country offices. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified significant gaps in existing knowledge that require primary research. Despite the widespread practice of labor augmentation globally, the evidence base remains weak, with most recommendations supported by low or very low-quality evidence. According to the GRADE methodology, further research is likely to impact recommendations based on low-quality evidence, while recommendations supported by moderate or high-quality evidence may not require immediate further research. Research priorities were determined based on originality, feasibility, potential to promote equity, and the likelihood of improving intrapartum care. Key research priorities include comparing the effects of oxytocin alone, amniotomy alone, and concurrent oxytocin and amniotomy in women with confirmed delays in the first stage of labor. The sequence of these interventions and their impact on outcomes also need to be studied. Additionally, the effects of antispasmodic agents for treating delayed labor and the use of amniotomy alone in women with a scarred uterus (e.g., due to previous cesarean section or myomectomy) require further investigation. The successful implementation of evidence-based policies for labor augmentation depends on well-planned, participatory processes for adapting and integrating the guidelines into national programs and health services. This may involve developing or revising national guidelines or protocols to meet the specific needs of each country. Modifications to the recommendations should be limited to weak recommendations, with explicit and transparent justifications for any changes. An enabling environment should be created to support the adoption of these practices, including behavioral changes among healthcare practitioners and managers. Monitoring and evaluating the implementation of the recommendations is essential. This can be achieved through clinical audits, interrupted time series, or criterion-based audits. Indicators such as the proportion of augmented labor cases, vaginal birth rates among women undergoing augmentation, and cesarean section rates for delayed labor should be tracked. These indicators provide insights into the overall use and success of labor augmentation practices and can be compared to local cesarean section rates. The WHO guideline will be updated five years after publication or sooner if new evidence necessitates revisions.
